title: Measuring GPU Memory Traffic on the NVIDIA GB10 Without C2C Telemetry
authors: Deepak Panigrahy; Sirisha Kota; Aakash Tyagi; David Kebo; Rabi Mahapatra
abstract: The NVIDIA GB10, used in the DGX Spark and in desktop AI systems from several vendors, joins an Arm CPU die and a Blackwell GPU die with NVLink C2C. The GPU has no local memory, so every GPU access that misses in its L2 cache crosses C2C to the LPDDR5X attached to the CPU die. Yet the software on the systems we tested exposes no counter for this traffic. We show that five L2 sector counters of the GPU, sampled every 10 ms through NVIDIA's CUPTI sampling interface by a process that does not attach to the workload, measure GPU memory traffic live and separate copy engine traffic from the read misses and writes of GPU kernels. For large streaming transfers of known size, the counters agree within 0.28% on an Acer GN100 and within 0.005% on a DGX Spark, track the volume moved regardless of how it is split into copies, and exclude data reused in L2. The GPU's SMMU counter, a natural alternative, counts address translations rather than bytes. Applied to an unmodified server, the method shows Mistral 7B decode reading 13.47 GiB per token, the weights it uses plus its key value (KV) cache, at 83% of the memory bandwidth NVIDIA specifies. We release the method as an open source tool.

title: ANOR: Scaling Sparse Attention with a GPU-PNM Computing Hierarchy
authors: Hyunsu Ye; Hyunmin Choi; Jaehong Cho; Jaeseo Lee; Hyeongseok Gwak; Joohee Lee; Donguk Moon; Woosuk Chung; Hoshik Kim; Kiwan Maeng; Jongse Park
abstract: Serving large language models with long contexts requires keeping the key-value (KV) cache of every request, which can exceed GPU memory capacity. Sparse attention reads only a small, query-dependent subset of this cache at each decoding step, yet must retain the full cache because later steps may select other entries. Processing-near-memory (PNM) devices attached through Compute Express Link (CXL) can hold the full cache and compute attention where it resides. Prior GPU-PNM systems for sparse attention are PNM-centric, processing most of the attention on the PNM. As existing CXL-PNM devices provide far less memory bandwidth than GPU HBM, this PNM-centric execution makes the PNM the bottleneck and leaves the GPU idle waiting for attention results. authors: Yong Li; Haoyu Wang; Kan Liu; Tao Lan
abstract: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. abstract: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. title: DyLoMo-DiT: Dynamic Looped Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Transformers
authors: Lernie Li; Yuanliu Liu; Pengfei Xiong; Wei Zhang
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. authors: Ziqing Ge
abstract: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. title: PackLoop: Row-Packed Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models under Concurrency
authors: Runguo Li; Dezhen Lu
abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
authors: Xuanya Zhu; Da Li; Xiatian Zhu
abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. authors: Xuyuan Xiong; Siyu Chen; Mengzhao Chen; Yue Su; Zhuoran Yang; Ping Luo; Xihui Liu
abstract: During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. title: When Does Decomposition Help? Empirical Study on Workload-Architecture Affinity in LLM Inference Serving
authors: Jihui Yang; Wentai Wu; Jiahua Huang; Weiwei Lin; Ligang He; Linghong Tsang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference can be organized as independent monolithic replicas, tensor- or pipeline-parallel serving groups, or disaggregated prefill and decode services. Although decomposition is often presented as a route to higher efficiency, its benefit depends on workload shape, model fit, and whether phase-specific resources can be independently scaled. Existing comparisons frequently change several of these factors at once. title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
authors: Jon Irureta; Jon Imaz; Philipp Wiesner; Gorka Azkune; Javier Fernandez-Marques; Alex Iacob; Andrej Jovanović; Aizea Lojo; Nicholas D. Lane
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies.
